Triggers.value: Specific body parts associated with the event
Night-time or waking up in the dark

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to sleep or lying in the dark

Memory.value: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

issues.item: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
issues.explanation: 'Always plan an escape route before entering a place' implies a persistent current external-danger / entrapment threat style that is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on intrusive sensory memory linked to the child's illness (body parts, darkness, songs; reliving, fragments, present-tense memory). For trauma of a child's life-threatening illness, this strategy is clinically much less coherent than avoidance/sleep delay, and it is not supported by any Threat or Appraisal items. Given the formulation, Triggers and Memory are strongly linked, but this item reflects a different syndrome focus (situational escape/safety behavior) not represented elsewhere in the selected nodes.

vignette: Chan's life fractured when his seven-year-old son was rushed from their rice paddy fields to the regional trauma center with fulminant meningitis. For eleven days, Chan stood beside a narrow hospital cot, watching the pediatric intensivist adjust the ventilator tubes and track the jagged green lines on the oscilloscope. The boy's pale, mottled skin, the rhythmic hiss of the respirator, and the hospital's soft chime of emergency songs became etched into Chan's nervous system. He watched his son fight for every breath under the glare of surgical lights and the absolute silence of the corridor at 3 a.m., when the monitors grew alarmingly flat before spiking again. The event anchored him in a landscape of medical urgency, making ordinary sensory inputs instantly dangerous. The moment Chan returned to the farm, the sight of his own calloused hands gripping the irrigation valves or the sudden crackle of his truck's radio playing a familiar ballad would instantly pull the hospital ward back into his mind. These cues collapsed time entirely, dragging the memory of his son's labored breathing and the stark, clinical angles of his boy's arms and neck into his immediate perception. Chan found himself bracing for the ventilator's hiss, certain the frightened event was unfolding right before him rather than resting behind months. The memory felt as present and urgent as the first night on the ward, overriding his sense of safety before he could even process the quiet of his own property. Because those sensory flashes arrived so suddenly and carried the weight of imminent loss, Chan began structuring his days to outrun them. He stopped answering the county agricultural cooperative's calls and declined invitations from neighbors who visited with harvest yields, fearing that ordinary conversations might accidentally brush against the hospital songs or the sight of a child's limbs. He took to delaying sleep until well past two in the morning, convincing himself that staying awake while his wife slept was the only way to keep the dread at bay. By lying in the dark on the edge of his mattress rather than surrendering to rest, he tried to maintain the hypervigilant stance he had learned on those hospital rounds. The relentless nature of these present-tense recollections dictated his daily avoidance, as each time the memory surfaced-feeling less like a recollection and more like an active threat-Chan's instinct was to isolate himself further. When fragments of the trauma appeared without warning, showing only the boy's IV line or a patch of darkened skin before vanishing, Chan would immediately retreat to the tool shed, shutting the heavy door and refusing to speak to anyone who knocked. Every time the memory of his son's critical hours surged back, demanding the same hypervigilance as the ward, Chan retreated further, proving once again how the memory dictated his avoidance. His attempts to delay sleep and avoid lying in the dark were desperate maneuvers to starve the memory of the rest it needed to fade, leaving him chronically exhausted but emotionally numb. Over time, the frequency of these intrusions did not dull; instead, it sharpened his awareness of anything that resembled the ward. The more often Chan's mind reconstructed the scene of his son's critical hours, the more acutely he began tracking environmental cues. Each new fragment of the memory acted as a lens, pulling the hospital's visual body parts and dark corridors into his present awareness, ensuring that the triggers he tried to outrun kept catching up to him. A neighbor's child coughing at a fence line or the distant wail of a tractor's backup alarm would instantly register as a signal of danger, hijacking his attention and reinforcing the idea that the threat was still active. His psychological landscape became a minefield where the memory itself acted as the detector, flagging new triggers that his exhausted mind could not filter. Chan's refusal to sleep and his withdrawal from community life ultimately manufactured the very conditions that kept the trauma alive. By remaining awake through the night and avoiding the restorative rhythm of ordinary social contact, he left his nervous system in a state of prolonged alertness, which in turn made every passing shadow or distant melody feel immediately potent. His isolation manufactured the very triggers he feared, creating a loop where his avoidance fed his memories, and his memories fed his avoidance, tightening around him like a vice. He finally agreed to seek help not because the fear had lessened, but because the weight of the cycle had begun to fracture his ability to manage the farm's irrigation schedule, leaving him desperate for a way to rest without feeling like his son was slipping away again.
